taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes populations south of the Gila River in southwestern Arizona and northwestern Sonora are now recognized as a separate species, P. goodei, and discusses possible cryptic diversity within P. platyrhinos.
fieldMarks: Flat, round body with horns and bumps; colour beige, tan, brown or slightly reddish to match the local soil.
Long head spines; 2.5-3.75 inches total (NPS Zion key); similar to the short-horned lizards but found at low elevations.
behavior: Ant specialist: bulk of the diet is large harvester ants; also other insects, spiders and some plant material.
Active mostly by day from about March, scarce above ground after mid-July in southern Nevada; buries itself in soil or uses burrows when inactive or too hot.
Not fast; relies on camouflage, and can inflate its body when pursued.
Egg layer: females bury eggs in soil; average clutch about 7; one or two clutches a year.
habitat: Desert shrublands (sagebrush, shadscale, hopsage, creosotebush, greasewood) on sandy flats, alluvial fans, washes and dune edges.
Most consistently where bare ground lies among open shrubs; found in sandy or gravelly valleys in Nevada.
range: Southeastern Oregon, southwestern Idaho and northern Utah south through eastern and southern California, Nevada and western Arizona to northeastern Baja California; from below sea level to about 1,980 m.
